body:
Childhood & Early Life

Philip Sidney was born in November 1554 at Penshurst Place in Kent, into the kind of family that lived close to the throne. His father Henry was a long-serving Lord Deputy of Ireland, his mother Mary Dudley was the sister of Elizabeth's favourite, the Earl of Leicester, and Queen Elizabeth was among those linked to his christening. He went to Shrewsbury School, where he met Fulke Greville, who became his closest friend and later his biographer, then to Oxford, though he left without a degree, as many gentlemen did.

At seventeen he was sent on a grand tour of Europe. In Paris in August 1572 he was staying at the English ambassador's house when the St Bartholomew's Day massacre began, and he watched Protestants being hunted through the streets. It marked him for life; he came away a committed Protestant and a believer in a European Protestant alliance against Spain.

What He Did & Why He's Remembered

Sidney was a courtier, soldier and diplomat first, and a poet almost in secret. None of his major work was printed in his lifetime. He circulated it in manuscript among friends, as a gentleman was supposed to. After his death it became the foundation of Elizabethan poetry. Astrophil and Stella was the first great English sonnet sequence, and it set off the whole craze that produced Spenser, Shakespeare and Daniel. His Defence of Poesy is the first major work of English literary criticism, arguing that poetry teaches by delighting. His prose romance Arcadia was one of the most read books of the age.

Family Life

His sister Mary, later Countess of Pembroke, was his closest literary ally. He wrote the Arcadia for her at her house in Wilton, and after his death she edited and published his work and finished the verse translation of the Psalms that the two of them had begun together. In 1583 he married Frances Walsingham, the daughter of Elizabeth's spymaster. They had one daughter, Elizabeth, born in 1585. Sidney was knighted the same year he married, mostly so that he could stand proxy for a German prince at a ceremony.

Romantic Life

The love story that made him famous is about Penelope Devereux, the clever, golden-haired daughter of the Earl of Essex. When Sidney was a young man, her dying father had apparently wished the two to marry, but nothing came of it. Sidney did not press the matter. In 1581 Penelope was married to Lord Rich, a match she is said to have hated. Only afterwards did Sidney begin writing as Astrophil, "star-lover", to Stella, "star". Whether the passion was entirely real or partly literary game is argued over to this day, but the poems are full of regret about the chance he let pass, and of a man writing his heart into verse because nothing else will help him. Penelope's later life was scandalous and difficult, and she left Rich for another lover.

Life Until Death

In 1585 he was made governor of Flushing and sent with Leicester's army to fight Spain in the Netherlands. On 22 September 1586 at the battle of Zutphen he rode into the fight without wearing leg armour, apparently out of some point of honour, and a musket ball broke his thigh. He was carried off the field and the wound turned gangrenous. The famous story, told by Fulke Greville, is that while he lay thirsty he passed a cup of water to another wounded soldier, saying "Thy necessity is yet greater than mine." He lingered for three weeks and died at Arnhem on 17 October 1586, aged thirty-one. England mourned him with a state funeral at St Paul's that was hardly ever matched for a private subject.

His Works

Below are four sonnets from Astrophel and Stella, in the old spelling of the 1591 printing as given in the Renascence Editions text. The first is the opening, in which a poet who cannot find words is told by his Muse to stop copying others and write from the heart. The second is the moon sonnet, one of the most loved in the language. The third is his prayer to sleep. The last is a quiet argument that those who say least love hardest.

Sonnet 1
LOuing in trueth, and fayne in verse my loue to show,
That she, deare Shee, might take som pleasure of my paine,
Pleasure might cause her reade, reading might make her know,
Knowledge might pittie winne, and pity grace obtaine,
I sought fit wordes to paint the blackest face of woe;
Studying inuentions fine, her wits to entertaine,
Oft turning others leaues, to see if thence would flow
Some fresh and fruitfull showers vpon my sun-burnd brain.
But words came halting forth, wanting Inuentions stay;
Inuention, Natures childe, fledde step-dame Studies blowes;
And others feet still seemde but strangers in my way.
Thus, great with childe to speak, and helplesse in my throwes,
Biting my trewand pen, beating myselfe for spite,
Fool, said my Muse to me, looke in thy heart, and write.
Sonnet 31
With how sad steps, O Moone, thou climbst the skies!
How silently, and with how wanne a face!
What, may it be that euen in heau'nly place
That busie archer his sharpe arrowes tries?
Sure, if that long-with-loue-acquainted eyes
Can iudge of loue, thou feel'st a louers case,
I reade it in thy lookes: thy languist grace,
To me that feele the like, thy state discries.
Then, eu'n of fellowship, O Moone, tell me,
Is constant loue deem'd there but want of wit?
Are beauties there as proud as here they be?
Do they aboue loue to be lou'd, and yet
Those louers scorn whom that loue doth possesse?
Do they call vertue there vngratefulnesse?
Sonnet 39
Come, Sleepe! O Sleepe, the certaine knot of peace,
The baiting-place of wit, the balme of woe,
The poor mans wealth, the prisoners release,
Th' indifferent iudge betweene the high and low!
With shield of proofe shield me from out the prease
Of those fierce darts Despaire at me doth throw.
O make in me those ciuil wars to cease;
I will good tribute pay, if thou do so.
Take thou of me smooth pillowes, sweetest bed,
A chamber deafe of noise and blind of light,
A rosie garland and a weary hed:
And if these things, as being thine in right,
Moue not thy heauy grace, thou shalt in me,
Liuelier then else-where, *Stellaes* image see.
Sonnet 54
Because I breathe not loue to euery one,
Nor doe not vse sette colours for to weare,
Nor nourish speciall locks of vowed haire,
Nor giue each speech a full point of a grone,
The Courtly Nymphes, acquainted with the mone
Of them wich in their lips Loues Standard beare:
What, he! (say they of me): now I dare sweare
He cannot loue; no,no, let him alone.
And thinke so still, so *Stella* know my minde;
Profess in deede I do not *Cupids* art;
But you, fair maides, at length this true shall find,
That his right badge is but worne in the hart:
Dumbe Swans, not chattering Pyes, do louers proue;
They loue indeed who quake to say they loue.
epi: Courtier, soldier and the first great English sonnet writer
quote: Fool, said my Muse to me, looke in thy heart, and write.
